The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

This metric induces the product topology: each coordinate projection is continuous from the bound on its summand, and a product neighborhood restricting finitely many coordinates contains a sufficiently small D-ball. Conversely, given a D-ball radius, make the geometric tail less than half that radius and restrict the finitely many remaining coordinates so their summands total less than the other half; this gives a product neighborhood inside the D-ball. A D-Cauchy sequence is Cauchy in each coordinate, so coordinate completeness gives a limit in S; bounding the first finitely many coordinate terms and then the geometric tail proves convergence in D. Sequences of rational vectors which are zero after finitely many coordinates form a countable dense subset, since the tail is arbitrarily small and each of finitely many coordinates can be approximated by rationals. Thus S is complete and separable, hence Polish by definition.

Set $Q_1=\pi_1$, the probability on the first two coordinates. For $N\ge2$, assume $Q_{N-1}$ is a probability on coordinates $1,\ldots,N$ with adjacent pair marginals $\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_{N-1}$ and last marginal $\mu_{n_N}$. Regard it as a law on $\mathbb R^{d(N-1)}\times\mathbb R^d$, and regard $\pi_N$ as a law on $\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d$; they have the common second/first marginal $\mu_{n_N}$. Define $\eta_N=(I_N)_\#Q_N$, that is, $\eta_N(B)=Q_N(I_N^{-1}(B))$ for Borel $B\subset S$. By [F7] it is a Borel probability, and its first $N+1$ coordinates have law $Q_N$ while every later coordinate equals zero.

The $j$th marginal of any $\eta_N$ is either $\mu_{n_j}$ (when $N+1\ge j$) or $\delta_0$. Hence $(\eta_N)$ is tight. By [F2] and Prokhorov, a subsequence converges weakly to a probability $\eta$ on $S$.

For fixed $k$, all sufficiently late $\eta_N$ have their $(k,k+1)$ coordinate marginal equal to $\pi_k$. > Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

derivations.claim: Suppose $W_2(\mu_n,\mu)\to0$. For each $n$ choose an optimal coupling $\pi_n$ and regard its coordinates as $X_n,Y$ with laws $\mu_n,\mu$. The cost gives $\int|X_n-Y|^2d\pi_n\to0$. For bounded continuous $\varphi$, choose a ball $B(0,K)$ with $\mu(B(0,K)^c)$ small. On the event $|Y|\le K$ and $|X_n-Y|\le\delta<1$, both points lie in the compact ball $\overline B(0,K+1)$, where $\varphi$ is uniformly continuous. The complement has probability at most $\mu(B(0,K)^c)+\delta^{-2}\int|X_n-Y|^2d\pi_n$. First choose $K$, then $δ$, and then $n$; the boundedness of $\varphi$ shows $\int\varphi d\mu_n-\int\varphi d\mu\to0$. Thus $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$.

Conversely suppose narrow convergence and the stated uniform tail condition. Fix $\varepsilon>0$. Choose $R$ so that the second-moment tails outside $Q=[-R,R]^d$ of all $\mu_n$ and of $\mu$ are less than $\varepsilon$; the tail of $\mu$ vanishes because $\mu\in\mathcal P_2$. Enlarge R slightly if necessary so its coordinate faces have zero $\mu$-mass. Partition each coordinate interval $[-R,R]$ by finitely many levels that are not atoms of the corresponding one-dimensional marginal of $\mu$, with mesh small enough that each resulting rectangular cell has diameter at most $\varepsilon$. Such levels exist because each probability has at most countably many atoms. Together with $Q^c$, these cells form a finite Borel partition $(C_i)_{i=0}^N$ whose boundaries have $\mu$-measure zero. By [F2], $a_{n,i}:=\mu_n(C_i)\to a_i:=\mu(C_i)$ for each $i$.

Write $Z_n=X_n-Y$ and $a_n=\int|Z_n|^2d\pi_n\to0$. For $R>K$, on $\{|X_n|>R\}$ either $|Y|>K$ or $|Z_n|>R-K$. Since $|X_n|^2\le2|Y|^2+2|Z_n|^2$, for every $n$, $\int_{|X_n|>R}|X_n|^2d\pi_n\le 2\int_{|Y|>K}|Y|^2d\pi_n+2K^2\frac{a_n}{(R-K)^2}+2a_n.$ Given a target $\eta>0$, first choose K so the first term is below $\eta/4$; then choose N so $a_n<\eta/8$ for $n\ge N$; then choose R>K so the middle term is below $\eta/8$ for all $n\ge N$. The last term is below $\eta/4$. Finally enlarge R so the finitely many tails for $n<N$ are below $\eta$. This proves the required uniform tail limit.

For each bounded cell $C_i\subset Q$, match mass $r_{n,i}=\min(a_{n,i},a_i)$. If $r_{n,i}>0$, take $r_{n,i}$ times the product of the probability measures $\mu_n|_{C_i}/a_{n,i}$ and $\mu|_{C_i}/a_i$; if $r_{n,i}=0$, use the zero measure. This gives a coupling piece supported on $C_i\times C_i$ with cost at most $\varepsilon^2r_{n,i}$. Subtract its two marginals from $\mu_n$ and $\mu$. The residual measures have equal mass. If that mass is positive, their normalized product, multiplied by that mass, couples them; if it is zero there is no residual piece. The sum is a coupling $\pi_n$ of $\mu_n,\mu$. Its matched cost is at most $\varepsilon^2$. For the residual coupling, $|x-y|^2\le2|x|^2+2|y|^2$. Its residual second moments are bounded by the two tails outside $Q$ plus $dR^2\sum_{i=1}^N|a_{n,i}-a_i|$ on each side: inside a bounded cell, unmatched mass is exactly the positive part of the difference of its two cell masses. Therefore $W_2(\mu_n,\mu)^2\le\int|x-y|^2d\pi_n\le\varepsilon^2+4\varepsilon+4dR^2\sum_{i=1}^N|a_{n,i}-a_i|.$ For this fixed finite partition the sum tends to zero, so $\limsup_nW_2(\mu_n,\mu)^2\le\varepsilon^2+4\varepsilon$. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ proves $W_2(\mu_n,\mu)\to0$.

For the witness, the mass outside a ball of radius $R$ is at most $n^{-2}$ for indices $n>R$ and is zero for indices $n\le R$; hence the family is tight. For bounded continuous $\varphi$, $\int\varphi d\mu_n=(1-n^{-2})\varphi(0)+n^{-2}\varphi(ne_1)\to\varphi(0)$, proving narrow convergence. Every coupling with second marginal $\delta_0$ is concentrated on $\mathbb R^d\times\{0\}$, so its cost is forced to be $\int|x|^2d\mu_n=1$. The asserted failure of W2 convergence follows.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)).

Let $a<b$ and let $f\in L^1([a,b])$. Define
$$F(x):=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt\qquad(a\le x\le b).$$
Then $F$ is differentiable for almost every $x\in(a,b)$ and
$$F'(x)=f(x)$$
at every such point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and

   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

derivations.claim: Let $D=\mathbb Q\cap[0,T]$ together with $0,T$. For each $q\in D$, set $f_q(t)=W_2(\mu_t,\mu_q)$. The reverse triangle inequality and the assumed control give $|f_q(t)-f_q(s)|\le\int_s^t g(r)dr$, so $f_q$ is absolutely continuous. By [F1], it has a derivative almost everywhere, and because $g\in L^1$ by Holder, at common differentiability points of $f_q$ and $G(t)=\int_0^t g(r)dr$, difference quotients give $|f_q'(t)|\le g(t)$. Since $D$ is countable, outside one null set all these derivatives exist and are bounded by $g$. Define $m(t)=\sup_{q\in D}|f_q'(t)|$ there and set $m=0$ on the null set. Difference quotients along $h=1/n$ give measurable versions of the scalar derivatives, so $m$ is measurable; also $0\le m\le g$ almost everywhere and hence $m\in L^2(0,T)$.

For any $s,t$, continuity of the curve and density of $D$ imply $W_2(\mu_s,\mu_t)=\sup_{q\in D}|f_q(t)-f_q(s)|.$ The inequality from right to left is the reverse triangle inequality. For the other direction take $q_j\in D$ with $q_j\to s$; then $f_{q_j}(s)\to0$ and $f_{q_j}(t)\to W_2(\mu_t,\mu_s)$. For each q, [F1] and step 1.1 give $|f_q(t)-f_q(s)|\le\int_s^t|f_q'(r)|dr\le\int_s^t m(r)dr$. Taking the supremum proves $W_2(\mu_s,\mu_t)\le\int_s^t m(r)dr$.

The function $H(t)=\int_0^t m(r)dr$ is absolutely continuous, and [F1] gives $H'(t)=m(t)$ almost everywhere. At a time t where $H$ is differentiable and every $f_q$ is differentiable, step 2.1 gives $\limsup_{h\to0}\frac{W_2(\mu_{t+h},\mu_t)}{|h|}\le m(t),$ while $W_2(\mu_{t+h},\mu_t)\ge|f_q(t+h)-f_q(t)|$ gives a lower limit at least $|f_q'(t)|$ for every q. Taking the supremum yields a lower limit at least $m(t)$. Thus the metric derivative exists and equals $m(t)$ almost everywhere. The interval bound and square integrability follow from step 2.1 and $m\le g$.

Let h be any other nonnegative $L^2$ upper control. Repeating the scalar difference-quotient bound of step 1.1 with h gives $|f_q'(t)|\le h(t)$ almost everywhere for each q. Countability of D lets these inequalities hold off a single null set, so $m(t)\le h(t)$ there. By step 3.1, $|\dot\mu_t|=m(t)$ almost everywhere, proving leastness.

statement.

> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily

indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed

first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers

order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the

If $\gamma$ is absolutely continuous with square-integrable derivative, Cauchy--Schwarz [F4] on each interval gives $Q_P(\gamma)\le\int_0^T|\dot\gamma|^2dt$.

Suppose $C<\infty$. On interval-step functions $f(t)=c_i$ for $t_i<t<t_{i+1}$ define $\Lambda(f)=\sum_i c_i\cdot(\gamma(t_{i+1})-\gamma(t_i))$. Cauchy--Schwarz for the finite sums gives $|\Lambda(f)|\le\left(\sum_i|c_i|^2\Delta t_i\right)^{1/2}Q_P(\gamma)^{1/2}\le\sqrt C\|f\|_{L^2}.$ By [F1], interval-step functions are dense in $L^2$, so $\Lambda$ extends uniquely to a bounded linear functional on the real Hilbert space $L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^d)$.

By [F2]–[F3], Riesz represents $\Lambda$ by some $u\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^d)$. Taking the step function equal to a fixed vector c on $(s,t)$ and zero elsewhere gives $c\cdot(\gamma(t)-\gamma(s))=\int_s^t c\cdot u(r)dr$ for every $c$ and every interval. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ and every real $a>0$,
$$\frac{x^m}{\exp(ax)}\longrightarrow0\qquad(x\to+\infty).$$

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$) at which $g$ is differentiable
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of Sums, scalar multiples, products, absolute values, maxima, minima and quotients with nonvanishing denominator of continuous functions are continuous, as are constants, the identity and every polynomial function.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

(Axis-parallel rectangles in $\mathbb{R}^m$ and their volume). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of Half-open boxes in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and their volume, and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ (Assuming countable choice, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra containing every elementary set and $\lambda_n$ is a complete measure extending elementary volume).

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $A$
([[def-continuity-real]]) and let $K \subseteq A$ be **nonempty** and compact
([[def-open-cover-r]]). Then $\sup f[K]$ and $\inf f[K]$ exist and are
**attained**: there are $p, q \in K$ with

$$f(q) \;=\; \inf f[K] \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; \sup f[K] \;=\; f(p) \qquad \text{for every } x \in K .$$

Equivalently, the set $f[K]$ has a maximum and a minimum
([[def-max-min]]), namely $\max f[K] = f(p)$ and $\min f[K] = f(q)$.

**Nonemptiness of $K$ is a hypothesis, not an oversight.** For $K = \varnothing$
the set $f[K]$ is empty, and neither a supremum nor a maximum of the empty set
exists in this library ([[def-complete-ordered-field]] supplies suprema of
nonempty sets bounded above only).

For each $k\ge0$, repeated chain and product rules give $\phi^{(k)}(t)=P_k(1/t)e^{-1/t}$ on $t>0$ for a polynomial $P_k$: it holds with $P_0=1$, and if $u=1/t$ then differentiation replaces $P_k(u)$ by the polynomial $u^2(P_k(u)-P_k'(u))$. By [F1], this derivative tends to $0$ as $t\downarrow0$. Its difference quotient at $0$ is $uP_k(u)e^{-u}$ with $u=1/t$, which also tends to $0$ by [F1]; from the left it is zero. Induction therefore gives every derivative at $0$ equal to $0$ and continuous there, so $\phi$ is smooth on $\mathbb R$.

Set $\Phi(t)=\phi(t+1)\phi(1-t)$. By [F2], $\Phi$ is smooth. It vanishes for $t\notin[-1,1]$ and is positive for $-1<t<1$, so its support is $[-1,1]$. Let $I=\int_{\mathbb R}\Phi(t)\,dt$. The extreme-value bound [F3] makes $\Phi$ bounded on $[-1,1]$, so $I<\infty$. Since $\Phi(0)=e^{-2}>0$, continuity gives $\delta\in(0,1)$ with $\Phi(t)\ge e^{-2}/2$ on $[-\delta,\delta]$; [F3] gives $I\ge\delta e^{-2}>0$. Hence $\psi=\Phi/I$ is smooth, supported on $[-1,1]$, positive on $(-1,1)$, and has integral one.

Define $\rho_d(x_1,\ldots,x_d)=\prod_{j=1}^d\psi(x_j)$. Repeated coordinatewise chain and product rules give every partial derivative as $\prod_{j=1}^d\psi^{(\alpha_j)}(x_j)$ for its multi-index $\alpha$, so all partial derivatives are continuous. The function is nonnegative, vanishes outside $[-1,1]^d$, and is positive at every point of $(-1,1)^d$; therefore its support is exactly that closed cube.

For $d=1$, $\int\rho_1=1$ by step 2.1. By step 3.1, $\rho_d$ is a nonnegative Borel function supported in the compact cube. For $d\ge2$, split $\mathbb R^d=\mathbb R^{d-1}\times\mathbb R$. By [F4] and Tonelli, $\int\rho_d\,dx=(\int\rho_{d-1}\,dx)(\int\psi\,dt)$; the second factor is $1$ by step 2.1. Induction on $d$ proves $\int_{\mathbb R^d}\rho_d\,dx=1$.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

derivations.claim: Fix an initial pair $(s,x_0)$ and a closed ball $K=\overline B(x_0,r)$. On a sufficiently short one-sided interval $J$ adjoining $s$, absolute continuity of the integrals of $m_K,L_K$ gives $\int_Jm_K\le r$ and $\int_JL_K<1$. On continuous curves taking values in $K$, define $\Phi(X)(t)=x_0+\int_s^t b(q,X(q))dq,$ with the oriented integral when J lies to the left of s. The integrand is measurable because $q\mapsto(q,X(q))$ is continuous and b is Borel; it is integrable because $|b(q,X(q))|\le m_K(q)$ almost everywhere. The map preserves the closed sup-norm ball of radius r about the constant curve $x_0$, and $\|\Phi(X)-\Phi(Y)\|_\infty\le(\int_JL_K)\|X-Y\|_\infty$. By [F1] it has a unique fixed point. The integral FTC [F2] makes this curve absolutely continuous and a solution almost everywhere.

We first prove the scalar zero-derivative implication needed for uniqueness. Let $H:[a,c]\to\mathbb R$ be absolutely continuous with $H'=0$ outside a null set $N$ containing the endpoints. For $\varepsilon>0$ and $n\ge1$, let $E_n$ consist of all $x\in[a,c]$ such that $|H(y)-H(x)|\le\varepsilon|y-x|$ whenever $y\in[a,c]$ and $|y-x|<1/n$. Continuity of $H$ makes $E_n$ closed: pass to the limit in this inequality for each fixed y with $|y-x|<1/n$. These compact sets increase with n and cover $[a,c]\setminus N$. Partition $[a,c]$ into finitely many closed intervals of length less than $1/n$. On each interval I, the compact image $H(E_n\cap I)$ has diameter at most $\varepsilon|I|$, so covering it by its smallest containing interval gives $\lambda(H(E_n))\le\varepsilon(c-a)$. By [F8], the increasing union of the compact images has measure at most $\varepsilon(c-a)$, hence $\lambda^*(H([a,c]\setminus N))\le\varepsilon(c-a)$. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ makes this image null; [F7] makes $H(N)$ null as well. Thus the whole range of H is null, and the intermediate value theorem [F8] makes H constant. The singleton interval is immediate.

Any absolutely continuous solution Y on a compact interval with image in K satisfies its integral equation. Indeed, $f(q)=b(q,Y(q))$ is measurable and bounded almost everywhere by $m_K$, hence integrable. By [F2], $I(t)=\int_a^t f(q)dq$ is absolutely continuous and $I'=f$ almost everywhere. Each component of $Y-I$ is absolutely continuous by the finite-family definition (split a given tolerance between the two summands), and has derivative zero almost everywhere. Step 1.2 makes it constant. Therefore $Y(t)-Y(a)=\int_a^t b(q,Y(q))dq$ for every t, and subtraction gives the oriented version with any base time.

If two solutions have the same value at one time and remain in a compact K on a common compact interval, partition that interval into finitely many subintervals on which $\int L_K<1$. By step 2.1 both satisfy their integral equations. On each subinterval beginning at a time where the solutions agree, these equations bound their sup-norm difference by $(\int L_K)$ times itself, so the difference is zero. Induction over the partition proves uniqueness throughout the common interval. Their compatible union therefore defines a unique maximal locally absolutely continuous solution: every compact subinterval of its domain is covered by finitely many local solution intervals, on which the integral equation holds. Suppose a maximal endpoint $\tau$ lies in $(0,T)$ and there are times $t_n\uparrow\tau$ with $X(t_n)$ in a compact set K. Choose R with K contained in the ball $B_R(0)$, put $K_1=\overline B_{R+1}(0)$, and take n large enough that $\int_{t_n}^{\tau}m_{K_1}<1$. If the path first reaches the boundary of $K_1$ at some $r\in(t_n,\tau)$, it stays in $K_1$ on $[t_n,r]$, so $|X(r)-X(t_n)|\le\int_{t_n}^r m_{K_1}<1$, while $|X(r)-X(t_n)|\ge |X(r)|-|X(t_n)|\ge1$, a contradiction. Let $T>0$, $d\ge1$, and let $(\mu_t,v_t)$ be a narrowly continuous finite-action solution of the continuity equation on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d$, with space-time law $M(dt,dx)=dt\,\mu_t(dx)$. Put $a(t)=\int|v_t(y)|^2d\mu_t(y)$ and $N=\{t:a(t)=+\infty\}$. Then $a$ is measurable, $N$ is Borel and Lebesgue-null, and the Borel representative $\bar v(t,x)=0$ for $t\in N$ and $\bar v(t,x)=v(t,x)$ for $t\notin N$ agrees with $v$ $M$-almost everywhere. For $\varepsilon>0$, let $\rho_\varepsilon$ be the strictly positive centered Gaussian probability density with covariance $\varepsilon I_d$, and define
$$p_t^\varepsilon(x)=\int\rho_\varepsilon(x-y)d\mu_t(y),\quad j_t^\varepsilon(x)=\int\rho_\varepsilon(x-y)\bar v_t(y)d\mu_t(y),\quad v_t^\varepsilon(x)=j_t^\varepsilon(x)/p_t^\varepsilon(x).$$
Then $p_t^\varepsilon$ is a strictly positive smooth probability density for each $t$, $t\mapsto\mu_t^\varepsilon$ is narrowly continuous, $v_t^\varepsilon$ is Borel and locally Lipschitz in $x$ with local magnitude and Lipschitz bounds integrable in time, and $(\mu_t*\rho_\varepsilon,v_t^\varepsilon)$ solves the continuity equation. For almost every $t$,
$$\int|v_t^\varepsilon(x)|^2p_t^\varepsilon(x)dx\le\int|v_t(y)|^2d\mu_t(y).$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T>0$, let $d\ge1$, and let $b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ be Borel. Suppose that for every compact $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ there are nonnegative $m_K,L_K\in L^1(0,T)$ such that for almost every $t$, $|b(t,x)|\le m_K(t)$ and $|b(t,x)-b(t,y)|\le L_K(t)|x-y|$ for all $x,y\in K$. For each $(s,x_0)$ there is a unique maximal locally absolutely continuous solution $X(\cdot;s,x_0)$ of $\dot X=b(t,X)$ with $X(s)=x_0$, defined on an interval $I\subseteq[0,T]$ containing $s$. Here locally absolutely continuous means absolutely continuous on every compact subinterval of $I$, and maximal means that it has no locally absolutely continuous solution extension to a strictly larger interval in $[0,T]$; any maximal endpoint lying in $(0,T)$ can occur only if the trajectory leaves every compact subset of $\mathbb R^d$. If, in addition, $b(t,\cdot)$ is continuously differentiable for almost every $t$ and $D_xb$ has integrable local bounds, then the set of initial points whose trajectories exist between any fixed pair of times is open, its time map is one-to-one onto an open image with both map and inverse continuously differentiable, and the path map into the uniform path space is continuous on the set of trajectories existing through the full interval. On compact flow tubes the dependence on the starting time is locally absolutely continuous and satisfies $\partial_sX(t;s,x)=-D_xX(t;s,x)b(s,x)$ for almost every s, simultaneously for x in the tube. The spatial derivative $V_t=D_{x_0}X(t;s,x_0)$ satisfies $\dot V_t=D_xb(t,X_t)V_t$, $V_s=I_d$, almost everywhere.

Assume countable choice. If $P$ is Polish and $\mu$ is a Borel probability measure on $P$, then for every Borel $A\subseteq P$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is a compact $K\subseteq A$ with $\mu(A\setminus K)<\varepsilon$.

Assume Countable Choice. For every integer $d\ge1$ there is a nonnegative function $\rho_d:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ with continuous partial derivatives of every order, support exactly $[-1,1]^d$, strictly positive on $(-1,1)^d$, and Lebesgue integral $\int_{\mathbb R^d}\rho_d(x)\,dx=1$. Here the support is the closure of the set where the function is nonzero.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \varphi(x)\,dx = 1. $$

For $\varepsilon > 0$, define

$$ \varphi_\varepsilon(x) := \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon) \qquad(x \in \mathbb{R}^n). $$

The family $(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is the **mollifier family
generated by $\varphi$**.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be locally integrable, let
$\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ have mass $1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon$ be the associated mollifier. Then for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, the convolution

$$ (f*\varphi_\varepsilon)(x) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(y)\varphi_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy $$

is smooth, and for every multi-index $\alpha$,

$$ \partial^\alpha(f*\varphi_\varepsilon) = f*(\partial^\alpha \varphi_\varepsilon). $$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Assume countable choice. If $P$ is Polish and $\mu$ is a Borel probability measure on $P$, then for every Borel $A\subseteq P$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is a compact $K\subseteq A$ with $\mu(A\setminus K)<\varepsilon$.

A topological space is **Polish** when it is separable ([[def-separable-space]]) and completely metrizable: its topology is induced by some complete metric ([[lem-complete-remetrisation]]). No particular compatible complete metric or countable dense subset is part of the structure.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: Apply [F2] to $v^\varepsilon$ and denote by $D_t$ the open set of initial points whose trajectories exist from time 0 through t, and by $E_t=X_t^\varepsilon(D_t)$ its open image. Fix $t\in(0,T]$ and $f\in C_c^\infty(E_t)$. For $0\le r\le t$ and $x\in D_{r,t}$, the set of states whose trajectories exist from r to t, define $\psi(r,x)=f(X^\varepsilon(t;r,x))$; extend it by zero outside $D_{r,t}$. Since $\operatorname{supp}f$ is compactly contained in $E_t$, its backward images form a compact subset of the flow domain. Thus $\psi$ has compact spatial support uniformly in r, is continuously differentiable in x, and is absolutely continuous in r locally. The start-time derivative from [F2] and the flow identity give $\partial_r\psi=\nabla f(X(t;r,x))\cdot[-D_xX(t;r,x)v_r^\varepsilon(x)]=-v_r^\varepsilon(x)\cdot\nabla_x\psi$ almost everywhere.

For this fixed t define the restricted finite pushforward $
u_t$ on $E_t$ by $
u_t(B)=\mu_0^\varepsilon(\{x\in D_t:X_t^\varepsilon(x)\in B\})$ for Borel $B\subseteq E_t$. The set is Borel because $X_t^\varepsilon$ is continuous on the open domain $D_t$; preimages preserve disjoint unions, so $
u_t$ is a finite Borel measure of mass $\mu_0^\varepsilon(D_t)$. The weak continuity-equation identity extends from smooth compact tests to compactly supported tests that are $C^1$ in x and absolutely continuous in r with locally integrable time derivative: multiply by a time cutoff, convolve in time and space on a fixed compact neighborhood, and pass to the limit. The terms converge because $p^\varepsilon$ is locally bounded, $p^\varepsilon v^\varepsilon$ is locally integrable in time and space by finite action, and the test and its spatial gradient converge uniformly while its time derivative converges in $L^1$. Apply this extension to $\eta(r)\psi(r,x)$ from step 1.1 for every smooth compactly supported time cutoff $\eta$. The transport equation leaves $\int\eta'(r)F(r)dr=0$, so $F(r)=\int\psi(r,x)d\mu_r^\varepsilon(x)$ is constant on $(0,t)$. Continuity of the flow and of $\mu_r^\varepsilon$ extends the identity to r=0,t, giving $\int f(y)d\mu_t^\varepsilon(y)=\int f(X_t^\varepsilon(x))d\mu_0^\varepsilon(x)$ for every $f\in C_c^\infty(E_t)$. Uniform mollification extends equality to every $f\in C_c(E_t)$; both measures are finite, so uniform limits pass through their integrals. For a compact $K\subset E_t$, choose n sufficiently large that the closed $1/n$-neighborhood of K is compactly contained in $E_t$ and set $f_n(x)=\max\{0,1-n\operatorname{dist}(x,K)\}$. Then $f_n\in C_c(E_t)$ and $f_n\downarrow\mathbf1_K$, so [F6] gives $
u_t(K)=\mu_t^\varepsilon(K)$. By [F5], both finite Borel measures on the Polish space $E_t$ are inner regular; their agreement on compact sets therefore proves $
u_t=\mu_t^\varepsilon|_{E_t}$.

For every $r\in(0,T]$, step 2.1 gives equality of the restricted finite measures on $E_r$. Applying it to $y\mapsto\min\{N,|v_r^\varepsilon(y)|^2\}$ and letting $N\uparrow\infty$ by [F7] yields $\int_{D_r}|v_r^\varepsilon(X_r^\varepsilon(x))|^2d\mu_0^\varepsilon(x)=\int_{E_r}|v_r^\varepsilon(y)|^2d\mu_r^\varepsilon(y)\le\int|v_r^\varepsilon(y)|^2d\mu_r^\varepsilon(y)$. Let $\mathscr D=\{(r,x):x\in D_r\}$. This domain is relatively open in $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d$ and $(r,x)\mapsto X_r^\varepsilon(x)$ is continuous on it: cover any compact trajectory segment through $(r,x)$ by finitely many local flow neighborhoods from [F2] and patch their continuous dependence on the initial point; time continuity follows from the integral equation. Thus the integrand is Borel; extend it by zero off $\mathscr D$. Tonelli [F4] then gives $\int\!\int_0^{\min\{T,\tau(x)\}}|v_r^\varepsilon(X_r^\varepsilon(x))|^2dr\,d\mu_0^\varepsilon(x)\le\int_0^T\!\int|v_r^\varepsilon(y)|^2d\mu_r^\varepsilon(y)dr<\infty.$ Thus for $\mu_0^\varepsilon$-almost every x the path has finite squared speed integral up to its maximal endpoint. Holder then makes its total path length finite. Such a path is Cauchy at any finite endpoint; it cannot escape every compact set, contradicting [F2] if an endpoint lies in $(0,T)$. At T it has a finite limit and extends continuously to T. Thus $\mu_0^\varepsilon(D_T)=1$.

For each t, step 2.1 identifies $\mu_t^\varepsilon|_{E_t}$ with $
u_t=(X_t^\varepsilon)_\#(\mu_0^\varepsilon|_{D_t})$, where this restricted pushforward is the finite measure defined in step 2.1. Since $D_T\subseteq D_t$ and $\mu_0^\varepsilon(D_T)=1$ by step 3.1, $
u_t(E_t)=\mu_0^\varepsilon(D_t)=1$. Hence $\mu_t^\varepsilon(E_t)=1$, and the equality of restricted measures extends to all Borel subsets of $\mathbb R^d$. Because $D_t$ is open and $X_t^\varepsilon$ is continuous there, extend $X_t^\varepsilon$ to all of $\mathbb R^d$ by setting it to zero off $D_t$; this is Borel and its pushforward is $
u_t$ since $\mu_0^\varepsilon(D_t)=1$. Thus $\mu_t^\varepsilon=(X_t^\varepsilon)_\#\mu_0^\varepsilon$. This proves the claim for every t, with the unique flow given by [F2].

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

derivations.claim: Set $\varepsilon_n=1/n$. For each n, let $D_n$ be the Borel full-$\mu_0^{\varepsilon_n}$-measure set of initial points whose regularized flow paths exist on all of $[0,T]$. The map $F_n:D_n\to C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)$, $F_n(x)(t)=X_t^{\varepsilon_n}(x)$, is Borel by [F1]. Extend it by the zero path off $D_n$ and define $\eta_n=(F_n)_\#\mu_0^{\varepsilon_n}$; this is the law of a Borel random element and is a Borel probability. For every t, composition with evaluation gives $(e_t)_\#\eta_n=(X_t^{\varepsilon_n})_\#\mu_0^{\varepsilon_n}=\mu_t^{\varepsilon_n}$ by [F1]. The flow equation, the same marginal identity, and Tonelli give $\int\mathcal E(\gamma)d\eta_n(\gamma)=\int_0^T\!\int|v_t^{\varepsilon_n}(x)|^2d\mu_t^{\varepsilon_n}(x)dt\le A,$ where $A=\int_0^T\!\int|v_t(x)|^2d\mu_t(x)dt<\infty$. The path space C with the uniform metric is Polish: it is complete by the continuous-curve completeness fact, and rational polygonal paths are countable and dense. By [F2], the sequence of initial laws is tight. Given $\delta>0$, choose compact K with $\mu_0^{\varepsilon_n}(K^c)<\delta/2$ for all n, and choose R so $A/R<\delta/2$. The set $K_R=\{\gamma:\gamma(0)\in K,\ \mathcal E(\gamma)\le R\}$ is closed by [F3] and compact by Arzela–Ascoli: its paths obey $|\gamma(t)-\gamma(s)|\le\sqrt{R|t-s|}$ and $\sup_t|\gamma(t)|\le\sup_{x\in K}|x|+\sqrt{RT}$. Markov's inequality, which follows from $\mathbf1_{\{\mathcal E>R\}}\le\mathcal E/R$, gives $\eta_n(K_R)\ge1-\delta$. Thus $(\eta_n)$ is tight; [F2] gives a weakly convergent subsequence, still denoted $\eta_n$, with Borel probability limit $\eta$.

For each t, evaluation $e_t:C\to\mathbb R^d$ is continuous, so weak convergence and the marginal convergence $\mu_t^{\varepsilon_n}\Rightarrow\mu_t$ imply $(e_t)_\#\eta=\mu_t$. By [F3], $\mathcal E$ is nonnegative and lower semicontinuous. For each integer k define $g_k(\gamma)=\min\{k,\inf_{\zeta\in C}[\mathcal E(\zeta)+k\|\gamma-\zeta\|_\infty]\}$. The triangle inequality makes $g_k$ k-Lipschitz, $0\le g_k\le\mathcal E$, and $g_k$ increases with k. If $a<\mathcal E(\gamma)$, lower semicontinuity gives a neighborhood of $\gamma$ where $\mathcal E>a$; outside that neighborhood the term $k\|\gamma-\zeta\|_\infty$ exceeds a for all sufficiently large k. $$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

statement.

The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. The law of a random element is a probability measure makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in The Dirac set function at a point.

  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$

$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$
